subject: Creative Arts
source: NaCCA Creative Arts Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4–6 (September 2019)
accessibility: Read prompts and choices aloud when needed. Practical responses may use classroom materials, movement, speech or drawing.

indicators.statement: Explore and study the artworks of some international visual artists and analyse how their artworks reflect the history and culture of some communities in the world.
indicators.content_standard: B6.1.1.1 Generate ideas for artistic expression from people, culture, environment and topical issues.

skills.description: Identify the subject, artistic method and evidence in a work.
Study and describe in visual arts.
Use artistic evidence to explain a choice or improvement.

questions.stem: After studying Ibrahim Mahama's transformation of used materials, pupils make a map hanging from pieces of worn cloth with route marks. What is this work about?
options: A waterway shaping life in a city
The journeys of people and goods
Reducing single-use bottles
Repairing cloth to reduce waste
questions.answer: The journeys of people and goods
hints: Identify the action or subject at the centre.
questions.explanation: The described action centres on the journeys of people and goods.

questions.stem: After studying Ibrahim Mahama's transformation of used materials, pupils make a map hanging from pieces of worn cloth with route marks. Which detail could a learner point out in the work?
options: A curved arrow leading from tap to bottle
Tree shapes overlapping the roofs of stalls
Raised bridges spanning a blue strip
Route marks passing across the seams
questions.answer: Route marks passing across the seams
hints: Look for a detail the example actually describes.
questions.explanation: The evidence in the example is route marks passing across the seams.

questions.stem: After studying Ibrahim Mahama's transformation of used materials, pupils make a map hanging from pieces of worn cloth with route marks. Which method is used?
options: Folding card to make raised forms
Simplifying objects into a printed symbol
Layering silhouettes on a folding map
Joining worn pieces and stitching a route
questions.answer: Joining worn pieces and stitching a route
hints: Think about how the parts were made or performed.
questions.explanation: The example uses joining worn pieces and stitching a route to show the journeys of people and goods.

questions.stem: A picture shows a market long ago. Which detail could help you learn about work there?
options: The number of corners on its label
The day you visited the picture
The colour of the museum door
The tools in the sellers' hands
questions.answer: The tools in the sellers' hands
hints: Find evidence inside the picture.
questions.explanation: Find evidence inside the picture. The tools in the sellers' hands.

questions.stem: A rough rock and a smooth bottle appear in a drawing. What is the artist showing by changing the marks on their surfaces?
options: The price
Texture
The date
The title
questions.answer: Texture
hints: Imagine how each surface would feel.
questions.explanation: Imagine how each surface would feel. Texture.

questions.stem: After studying Ibrahim Mahama's transformation of used materials, pupils make a map hanging from pieces of worn cloth with route marks. Which idea does the work suggest?
options: Used materials can carry traces of journeys
Bottles can be filled again here
Crossings link neighbourhoods divided by water
Repair can extend the life of cloth
questions.answer: Used materials can carry traces of journeys
hints: Connect the detail to the idea it expresses.
questions.explanation: The detail of route marks passing across the seams supports the idea that used materials can carry traces of journeys.

questions.stem: After studying Ibrahim Mahama's transformation of used materials, pupils make a map hanging from pieces of worn cloth with route marks. Which source would help the class check its account?
options: A labelled plan and street view of the district studied
A partner school's photograph of a refill station
A credited interview about Ibrahim Mahama's choice of materials
A labelled street study from the African city shown
questions.answer: A credited interview about Ibrahim Mahama's choice of materials
hints: Choose evidence about the actual subject.
questions.explanation: The closest source for this subject is a credited interview about Ibrahim Mahama's choice of materials.

questions.stem: After studying Ibrahim Mahama's transformation of used materials, pupils make a map hanging from pieces of worn cloth with route marks. Which sentence describes evidence before giving an opinion?
options: The work will win first prize.
The maker must have found the work easy.
Route marks passing across the seams.
Everybody will like the finished piece.
questions.answer: Route marks passing across the seams.
hints: Choose a detail you can check in the example.
questions.explanation: Route marks passing across the seams. This detail can be checked without guessing what someone thinks.

questions.stem: Two prints have the same subject. One is made with bold blocks, the other with thin lines. What differs?
options: The number of subjects studied
The fact that both are prints
The way the subject is shown
The place named in both titles
questions.answer: The way the subject is shown
hints: Look at how the marks are made.
questions.explanation: Look at how the marks are made. The way the subject is shown.

questions.stem: A drawing shows tiny figures beside a large tree. Which part suggests the tree's size?
options: The frame is brown.
The figures are small beside it.
The paper has four corners.
The drawing has a title.
questions.answer: The figures are small beside it.
hints: Compare the sizes within the picture.
questions.explanation: Compare the sizes within the picture. The figures are small beside it.

questions.stem: Which question asks about an artist's method?
options: How did you put the parts of the work together?
Who opened the door for the visitors?
What day will the class go home?
How far is the hall from the road?
questions.answer: How did you put the parts of the work together?
hints: Method means the way something was made.
questions.explanation: Method means the way something was made. How did you put the parts of the work together?.

questions.stem: A visitor says a work feels joyful. What would turn this feeling into an explanation?
options: Point to a feature that gives that impression
Count the visitors who came in that day
Write the price next to the title
Repeat the word joyful more loudly
questions.answer: Point to a feature that gives that impression
hints: Connect a feeling to something in the work.
questions.explanation: Connect a feeling to something in the work. Point to a feature that gives that impression.

questions.stem: After studying Ibrahim Mahama's transformation of used materials, pupils make a map hanging from pieces of worn cloth with route marks. Which change would make the main detail easier to recognise?
options: Leave the canal visible under each raised span
Continue the route across each join so it can be followed
Make the end of the arrow visible inside the bottle
Leave parts of the stalls visible under the tree shapes
questions.answer: Continue the route across each join so it can be followed
hints: Keep the aim and strengthen the clue the audience needs.
questions.explanation: This change helps the audience notice route marks passing across the seams.

questions.stem: A pupil wants marks on a cloth hanging to suggest a journey through several places. Which design decision supports this?
options: Remove the route and use only the artist's name.
End every route at the first seam and cover the next piece.
Put all the marks inside a label hidden behind the hanging.
Continue one route across the joins between pieces.
questions.answer: Continue one route across the joins between pieces.
hints: Let the eye follow a connection across the work.
questions.explanation: Let the eye follow a connection across the work. Continue one route across the joins between pieces.

questions.stem: After studying Ibrahim Mahama's transformation of used materials, pupils make a map hanging from pieces of worn cloth with route marks. A partner wants to know why the artist chose this method. Which reply explains the choice?
options: It helps show the journeys of people and goods.
It proves this is the only way to make the piece.
It shows the artist used the most costly tools.
It guarantees that everyone will have the same feeling.
questions.answer: It helps show the journeys of people and goods.
hints: Ask what this choice helps the audience notice.
questions.explanation: Joining worn pieces and stitching a route helps communicate the subject through route marks passing across the seams.

questions.stem: A pot has a wide mouth and two handles. What might its handles help a person do?
options: Make it deeper
Change its colour
Lift the pot
Close its mouth
questions.answer: Lift the pot
hints: Look at the way hands could hold it.
questions.explanation: Look at the way hands could hold it. Lift the pot.

questions.stem: A museum label gives a maker, a place and a date. What can you learn from it?
options: Who made the work and where and when it was made
What every visitor felt when seeing it
How many works the maker will make next year
What colours the maker liked best as a child
questions.answer: Who made the work and where and when it was made
hints: Read what the label actually records.
questions.explanation: Read what the label actually records. Who made the work and where and when it was made.

questions.stem: A child says a painted clay bowl is both useful and decorative. Why?
options: Painting makes the bowl deeper.
It can hold things and its painted marks can be enjoyed.
It must cost twice as much.
All bowls have the same marks.
questions.answer: It can hold things and its painted marks can be enjoyed.
hints: Think about what the bowl does and how it looks.
questions.explanation: Think about what the bowl does and how it looks. It can hold things and its painted marks can be enjoyed.

questions.stem: Which pair of notes keeps an observation separate from a guess?
options: It must be old. It must cost a lot.
It must mean luck. Everyone must agree.
I notice a repeated shape. It might stand for people meeting.
It is the best. It is better than the rest.
questions.answer: I notice a repeated shape. It might stand for people meeting.
hints: State what can be noticed before suggesting a meaning.
questions.explanation: State what can be noticed before suggesting a meaning. I notice a repeated shape. It might stand for people meeting.

questions.stem: After studying Ibrahim Mahama's transformation of used materials, pupils make a map hanging from pieces of worn cloth with route marks. What do you notice about the journeys of people and goods? Describe one detail in the example and explain what it tells you about life in a community elsewhere in the world.
hints: Connect the detail to the idea it expresses.
questions.explanation: For example, connect route marks passing across the seams to the idea that used materials can carry traces of journeys. Other supported choices are welcome.

criteria.description: Identifies the subject in the example.
Describes a detail and links it to the subject or setting.

options: A curved arrow leading from tap to bottle
Tree shapes overlapping the roofs of stalls
Raised bridges spanning a blue strip
Route marks passing across the seams
questions.answer: Route marks passing across the seams

questions.explanation: The evidence in the example is route marks passing across the seams.

questions.stem: After studying Ibrahim Mahama's transformation of used materials, pupils make a map hanging from pieces of worn cloth with route marks. Which technique could a pupil borrow for a new idea?
options: Stitching and arranging fabric samples
Joining worn pieces and stitching a route
Simplifying objects into a printed symbol
Folding card to make raised forms
questions.answer: Joining worn pieces and stitching a route

questions.stem: You need three ideas for showing a tree. Which set gives three real alternatives?
options: Three copies of the same unchanged outline
Three prices for one pencil
A leaf rubbing, a cut-paper tree and a clay model
The same drawing signed three times
questions.answer: A leaf rubbing, a cut-paper tree and a clay model
hints: Change the way the subject is shown.
questions.explanation: Change the way the subject is shown. A leaf rubbing, a cut-paper tree and a clay model.

questions.stem: What can a collected leaf suggest for a pattern?
options: The shape of its edge or the branching of its veins
The length of the school day
The price of the drawing paper
A list of classmates' names
questions.answer: The shape of its edge or the branching of its veins
hints: Study the leaf's visible features.
questions.explanation: Study the leaf's visible features. The shape of its edge or the branching of its veins.

questions.stem: After studying Ibrahim Mahama's transformation of used materials, pupils make a map hanging from pieces of worn cloth with route marks. Which idea could still be shared in a different version?
options: Crossings link neighbourhoods divided by water
Used materials can carry traces of journeys
Bottles can be filled again here
Trees give shade to people working outdoors
questions.answer: Used materials can carry traces of journeys
hints: Connect the detail to the idea it expresses.
questions.explanation: The detail of route marks passing across the seams supports the idea that used materials can carry traces of journeys.

questions.stem: After studying Ibrahim Mahama's transformation of used materials, pupils make a map hanging from pieces of worn cloth with route marks. Which source could help a pupil develop the subject further?
options: A tailor explaining a repair in the town studied
A partner school's photograph of a refill station
A labelled plan and street view of the district studied
A credited interview about Ibrahim Mahama's choice of materials
questions.answer: A credited interview about Ibrahim Mahama's choice of materials

questions.explanation: The closest source for this subject is a credited interview about Ibrahim Mahama's choice of materials.

questions.answer: Route marks passing across the seams.

questions.explanation: Route marks passing across the seams. This detail can be checked without guessing what someone thinks.

questions.stem: Which choice develops a symbol for sharing?
options: Try two hands passing one bowl between them
Write a different date at every corner
Copy a picture of an empty wall
Draw the border first and leave the subject undecided
questions.answer: Try two hands passing one bowl between them
hints: Use a visible action to express the idea.
questions.explanation: Use a visible action to express the idea. Try two hands passing one bowl between them.

questions.stem: You want a new border based on waves. Which drawing develops the idea?
options: A square left empty beside the page
An unrelated list of boat names
A label with the date of the visit
A row of curved marks that rise and fall
questions.answer: A row of curved marks that rise and fall
hints: Find a visual feature of waves that can repeat.
questions.explanation: Find a visual feature of waves that can repeat. A row of curved marks that rise and fall.

questions.stem: Which action helps a group begin with several possible ideas?
options: Let each person suggest a different way to show the theme
Choose the first suggestion before anyone else speaks
Wait until the finished work is on display
Use the title as the whole design
questions.answer: Let each person suggest a different way to show the theme
hints: Think of more than one starting point.
questions.explanation: Think of more than one starting point. Let each person suggest a different way to show the theme.

questions.stem: Which research question could inspire a new work about a place?
options: What is the price of the display tape?
How many letters are in our classroom number?
What details would someone who lives here notice?
Which seat will the teacher use?
questions.answer: What details would someone who lives here notice?
hints: Ideas often begin with noticing something specific.
questions.explanation: Ideas often begin with noticing something specific. What details would someone who lives here notice?.

questions.stem: After studying Ibrahim Mahama's transformation of used materials, pupils make a map hanging from pieces of worn cloth with route marks. Which suggestion develops the existing idea?
options: Continue the route across each join so it can be followed
Leave parts of the stalls visible under the tree shapes
Leave the canal visible under each raised span

End every route at the first seam and cover the next piece.
Remove the route and use only the artist's name.
Continue one route across the joins between pieces.
questions.answer: Continue one route across the joins between pieces.
hints: Let the eye follow a connection across the work.
questions.explanation: Let the eye follow a connection across the work. Continue one route across the joins between pieces.

questions.stem: After studying Ibrahim Mahama's transformation of used materials, pupils make a map hanging from pieces of worn cloth with route marks. A partner wants to know why the artist chose this method. Which reply explains the choice?
options: It helps show the journeys of people and goods.

questions.answer: It helps show the journeys of people and goods.

questions.explanation: Joining worn pieces and stitching a route helps communicate the subject through route marks passing across the seams.

questions.stem: A pupil wants to show that one figure is important. Which sketch is worth trying?
options: Hide that figure behind the frame
Give that figure more space than the others
Draw only the title and leave out all figures
Make every part equally hard to see
questions.answer: Give that figure more space than the others
hints: Think about what attracts the eye.
questions.explanation: Think about what attracts the eye. Give that figure more space than the others.

questions.stem: A class likes the repeated pattern in another artist's work. How can it use the idea in its own work?
options: Say the original was made by the class
Repeat a new shape or sound chosen for its own subject
Trace all the details and sign the artist's name
Change only the price on the original label
questions.answer: Repeat a new shape or sound chosen for its own subject
hints: Borrow a way of working and make new choices.
questions.explanation: Borrow a way of working and make new choices. Repeat a new shape or sound chosen for its own subject.

questions.stem: You like the woven lines on a basket. Which idea uses that observation in a new design?
options: Trace the whole basket label
Copy the price from the shelf
Draw crossing bands on a paper bookmark
Use the maker's name as your own
questions.answer: Draw crossing bands on a paper bookmark
hints: Borrow a visible feature for a different use.
questions.explanation: Borrow a visible feature for a different use. Draw crossing bands on a paper bookmark.

questions.stem: You have three ideas on separate cards. Two seem to tell parts of one story. What could you try?
options: Place them together and skip checking the result
Combine the two and check whether the story still makes sense
Remove both because they are similar
Choose a fourth idea without reading the cards
questions.answer: Combine the two and check whether the story still makes sense
hints: Check what the combination communicates.
questions.explanation: Check what the combination communicates. Combine the two and check whether the story still makes sense.

questions.stem: After studying Ibrahim Mahama's transformation of used materials, pupils make a map hanging from pieces of worn cloth with route marks. Use the example to invent two ideas for a visual artwork about the journeys of people and goods. Show one idea and say how it differs from the example.
hints: Connect the detail to the idea it expresses.
questions.explanation: For example, connect route marks passing across the seams to the idea that used materials can carry traces of journeys. Other supported choices are welcome.

criteria.description: Offers two ideas connected to the subject.
Develops and explains an original idea from the example.

options: Pick the story with the most characters
Ask what each person saw and compare their accounts
Put the two dates together as one date
Choose the story told in the loudest voice
questions.answer: Ask what each person saw and compare their accounts

The song its maker sang

questions.stem: Which question checks whether a work served its purpose?
options: Was it finished on the tallest desk?
Was the maker standing closest to the door?
Did it have more letters in its title?
Did its choices help the audience understand or do what the maker intended?
questions.answer: Did its choices help the audience understand or do what the maker intended?
hints: Compare the result with the aim.

questions.stem: How can two viewers disagree and both give useful comments?
options: Each can explain their view using a detail from the work.
They must write the same comment word for word.
They should ignore the work and vote about the maker.
They must choose the older viewer's opinion.
questions.answer: Each can explain their view using a detail from the work.

questions.stem: A class stages a play for partner schools about an online rumour. Actors pass a phrase down a line until a final actor checks the original notice. Which suggestion gives the maker a specific next step?

questions.stem: A drama follows a rumour as each actor changes one word. What ending gives an audience evidence of the change?
options: Show the final actor holding a blank card without speaking.
Speak the original notice and the final version so listeners can compare.
Have every actor say that all versions were identical.
End before the first notice is heard.
questions.answer: Speak the original notice and the final version so listeners can compare.
hints: The audience needs both versions to judge what changed.

questions.stem: A class stages a play for partner schools about an online rumour. Actors pass a phrase down a line until a final actor checks the original notice. A partner wants to know why the artist chose this method. Which reply explains the choice?
options: It guarantees that everyone will have the same feeling.

It helps show how a rumour changes as it travels.
It shows the artist used the most costly tools.
questions.answer: It helps show how a rumour changes as it travels.

questions.explanation: Passing altered lines between actors helps communicate the subject through the last actor comparing the phrase with the notice.

questions.stem: How can the group compare its first performance with a revision?

questions.stem: A group sings well together but the words disappear under a shaker. What feedback fits?

Keep the group singing and soften the shaker under the words.

questions.stem: What distinguishes a report of the event from a plan for it?
options: A report describes what actually happened and what people noticed.
